text: Hanoi, French colonial Vietnam. The French built new sewers under their part of town. Rats loved them. They came up through the toilets, and plague was spreading across Asia.
So in April 1902 the city opened a hunt for everyone: bring in a rat tail, get paid — reportedly one cent a tail. Just the tail. Nobody wanted piles of dead rats at the police station.
It worked... on paper. At the peak, over twenty thousand tails came in a single day.

Then officials started seeing rats running around with no tails. People had figured it out: cut off the tail, let the rat go, let it make more rats — and more tails. Inspectors even found rat farms outside the city.

The city wanted fewer rats. It paid for tails. So it got tails. The hunt failed, and the plague came anyway. Historian Michael Vann, who dug the story out of the colonial archives, calls it "absolutely a disaster."
